# Volunteer runs

<!-- generated by `python3 -m validation.volunteer docs`: edit the cards (validation/<case>/volunteer.json), not this file -->

Some validation cases need more computer than we have.  If you have cluster time, you can run one of them with five commands, knowing beforehand what it costs, and send back one small file.  We check that file mechanically: the mesh must be ours and the numbers must agree with each other.  The result is then judged against the case's pass/fail limits, fixed before any run, and reported whether it passes or not.  Contributed results are under the project's BSD-3 licence, and you are credited in the case's results.

**This is a trial.**  The volunteer framework is new: a test of whether people with more computing power can take the validation cases beyond what the maintainer can run on one desktop.  Expect rough edges, and tell us what went wrong (an issue) as well as what worked.

## The five commands

```bash
git clone --branch <tag> https://github.com/sigveka/hexmesh && cd hexmesh
pip install -e .
python3 -m validation.volunteer list                      # cases and their requirements
python3 -m validation.volunteer prepare <case> <level> --dir run/   # mesh, case, job script
sbatch run/job.sh        # or: bash run/job.sh  (resumable: run it again after a stop)
python3 -m validation.volunteer collect run/              # writes one .contrib.json
```

Send the `.contrib.json` file back: in a pull request, attached to the case's issue (label `volunteer-run`), or by e-mail.  Nothing else is needed.  `collect --name "Your Name" --machine "cluster, node type"` puts your credit in the file.

- **`<tag>`** is the release named in the card below: the mesh check needs the same hexmesh and gmsh versions.
- **OpenFOAM:** `prepare` uses the first of these it finds: `HEXMESH_OPENFOAM` if set; OpenFOAM already loaded (`module load …`, the `path` runner); the bashrc in `HEXMESH_OPENFOAM_RC`; Apptainer or Singularity with the card's image; Docker.  Choose one with `--runner path`, `--runner apptainer:docker://<image>` and so on.  It refuses another OpenFOAM version than the card's, unless you pass `--allow-version` (the version is recorded either way).
- **Cores:** `job.sh` asks for the card's recommended cores; `prepare --np N` changes that.  Under Slurm the run uses `SLURM_NTASKS`.
- **Stopping and resuming:** the run saves its state every 50 solver steps.  Run `job.sh` again after a stop; it continues from the last save.
- **What is sent back:** the level's numbers, the versions used, the mesh's fingerprint and check, cores, wall time and peak memory, and the last 200 lines of the solver log.  No fields, no mesh: well under 1 MB.

## Laminar flow in a helical pipe (`helical_pipe`)

Steady laminar flow through four turns of a helical coil (the SIET coil: 12.53 mm tube, 1 m helix diameter, 0.8 m pitch), meshed by hexmesh along a spline through the helix.  It checks that the friction factor converges as the mesh is refined and lands within 5 % of Ito's correlation.  Two of the three Reynolds numbers are done on the finest mesh; the last one, Re 3000, needs about 8 hours on 4 cores and several GB of memory, which our one desktop can't spare.

- **OpenFOAM:** v2406 (image `opencfd/openfoam-default:2406`)
- **hexmesh:** volunteer-helical-1 (git checkout volunteer-helical-1 before prepare: the mesh check needs the same meshing code as ours)
- **gmsh:** 4.12.1 (the version pip installs with hexmesh is fine: our test level's mesh check gives the same fingerprint with gmsh 4.12.1 and 4.15.2)

### Level `re3000_n24`: Re 3000 on the finest mesh (nang 24)

The run first solves the next-coarser mesh (nang 16, 0.8 million cells) and starts the fine one (2.7 million cells) from its mapped result, which shortens the fine solve.  Both stop when the solver converges (at most 5000 steps); the results are saved every 50 steps.

```bash
python3 -m validation.volunteer prepare helical_pipe re3000_n24 --dir run/
```

| requirement | value | basis | where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| cores (MPI processes) | 4 | measured | our runs of this level at Re 1800 and 2400 used 4 processes on one 8-core desktop; any count from 1 works, more is faster |
| wall time at 4 cores | 8.3 h | estimated | from the measured Re 2400 run at 4 processes (desktop, 2026-11-08: 563 coarse steps in 52 min, then 398 fine steps in 5.6 h, partly shared with another run), scaled by steps: at nang 16, Re 3000 needed 720/561 of Re 2400's steps |
| time to prepare (one core, no MPI) | 0.5 h | estimated | making the fine mesh measured 7 min (desktop, 2026-11-10); converting and checking it scaled by cells from the coarse mesh's measured 4.5 min; preparing the coarse start measured 8 min |
| peak memory | 3.4 GB | estimated | the solve at 4 processes peaked at 1.0 GB on the coarse mesh (0.8 million cells; desktop, 2026-11-10), scaled by cells to 2.7 million; making the fine mesh measured 3.2 GB (2026-11-10), and converting it is estimated at 2.5 GB the same way |
| peak disk | 4 GB | estimated | the fine case took about 1.6 GB in our runs (measured); while a 50-step chunk runs, its decomposed copy about doubles that; the coarse start's case is 0.25 GB (measured), deleted once mapped |
| cells | 2,711,232 | measured | the fine mesh's exact count (the coarse start has 803328) |

**Pass/fail limits** (fixed before any run; a result is reported whether it passes or not):

- the spline's distance from the exact helix (32 points per turn): within 0.1 % of $d$
- Darcy friction factor $f$, finest level, at Re 1800, 2400 and 3000: within 5 % of Ito (1959)
- mesh convergence of $f$ at each Re (nang 12, 16, 24): Richardson status converging; GCI reported
- reported, not gated: the digitised measured points (Fig. 12); f per pair of consecutive turns: reported

**Sent back:** one file, helical_pipe-<level>.contrib.json, about 100 kB
